extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers, students, and general readers seeking an overview of fiction-writing concepts
extracted.subtask_description: General guidance and evaluative dimensions for composing fictional prose (short stories, novellas, novels, screenplays), covering genre, core elements (character, plot, setting, theme, style), and authorial rules of craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre (genre fiction vs literary fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genre is the subject matter or category writers use (e.g., science fiction, fantasy, mystery). Genre fiction (popular fiction) is plot-driven and written to fit a specific literary genre to appeal to readers familiar with that genre. Literary fiction is fictional works that hold literary merit, offering social commentary or political criticism and focusing more on theme and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre fiction: storytelling driven by plot, commercial, meant to appeal to a large audience (example: Twilight). Literary fiction: analyzes reality, focuses on theme and character (example contrast: Moby-Dick). The distinction is controversial among critics. Use genre expectations to shape plot and audience appeal; use literary approaches to emphasize theme, character depth, and social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character / Characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization is one of the five elements of fiction (with plot, setting, theme, style). A character is a participant in the story and may be a person or any persona/entity originating from the fictional work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize character types: point-of-view character (the character by whom the story is viewed), protagonist (main character), antagonist (opposes protagonist), minor character (interacts with protagonist to help story move along), foil character (usually minor, traits opposed to main character). Use choices under pressure to reveal true character—Robert McKee: 'True character is revealed in the choices a human being makes under pressure—the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation.' Ensure every character wants something (Vonnegut rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (structure and scene/sequel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is the rendering and ordering of events and actions: initiating event, rising action, conflict, climax, falling action, and possibly resolution. Plot consists of action and reaction (stimulus and response) and has a beginning, middle, and ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mid-level structure: scene (unit of drama where action occurs) followed by sequel (emotional reaction and regrouping). The climax 'consists of a single action-packed sentence in which the conflict (problem) of the novel is resolved' and should come toward the end; the main part of the action should come before the climax. Ensure scenes advance action and sequels provide emotional consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is the locale and time of a story; sometimes called milieu to include broader context such as society beyond immediate surroundings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting may be real, a fictitious city/country, a different planet, or an alternate universe. Use setting to ground reader in where and when the story takes place and to contribute to mood, theme, and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Theme is what the author is trying to tell the reader (e.g., belief in the ultimate good in people, things are not always what they seem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theme is often the 'moral of the story'; some fiction contains advanced themes like morality or the value of life, while other stories have no theme or a very shallow one. Decide how explicit or subtle the theme should be based on genre and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style (voice and micro-level choices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style encompasses the multitude of conscious and unconscious choices writers make — strategic choices like point of view and narrator and tactical choices of grammar, punctuation, word usage, sentence and paragraph length and structure, tone, imagery, chapter selection, titles, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These choices meld to become the writer's voice. Attend to both high-level decisions (narrative perspective, tense) and low-level craft (sentence rhythm, diction, punctuation) to create consistent voice. Style choices should serve character, plot, and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator is the storyteller; the main character can also be the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a narrator whose knowledge, reliability, and perspective suit the story. The narrator's presence affects voice, point of view, and how information is revealed to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view is the perspective or 'lens' through which a story is communicated; narrative point of view describes the position of the narrator in relation to the story being told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an appropriate POV (first person, third person limited/omniscient, etc.) and maintain it consistently unless purposeful shifts are made. POV determines how much internal access readers have to characters and how events are filtered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone expresses the writer's attitude toward or feelings about the subject matter and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish tone early and maintain consistency appropriate to genre and theme. Tone affects word choice, sentence rhythm, and the reader's emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension of disbelief is the reader's temporary acceptance of story elements as believable, regardless of how implausible they may seem in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain suspension of disbelief, ensure internal consistency, believable character motivations, coherent worldbuilding, and clear cause–effect relationships even in fantastical settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description / Show, don't tell (Stephen King guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Description should begin in the writer's imagination but 'finish in the reader's' (Stephen King). The article also links to the principle 'Show, don't tell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evocative details that engage readers' senses and imagination, allowing them to infer and visualize rather than supplying all exposition. Give readers sufficient information as early as needed for understanding but avoid over-explaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kurt Vonnegut's rules for writing a successful story
rubrics_metrics.description: Vonnegut's eight rules (paraphrased from the page): 1) Use a stranger's time so it's not wasted. 2) Give the reader at least one character to root for. 3) Every character should want something. 4) Every sentence must reveal character or advance action. 5) Start as close to the end as possible. 6) Make awful things happen to reveal character. 7) Write to please one person (avoid pandering to everyone). 8) Give readers as much information as possible as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prescriptive maxims guide pacing, empathy, plot economy, conflict, and clarity. Examples/interpretation: focus narrative energy, ensure stakes, prioritize sentences that matter, aim for immediacy, and provide necessary context early to help reader understanding.
